summary: A revised set of ARPANET mailing lists for distributing network documents, replacing the one in RFC 329. List A lets sites reach network liaisons quickly with their own documents, while lists B and C are used by the Network Information Center for other participants and for station agents. It was replaced by RFC 402.

plainLanguage.summary: An updated address book of who should get printed copies of network notes, so every person on the list gets their mail.

subtitle: Updated mailing lists for distributing network documents as the ARPANET grew.

tldr.problem: By August 1972, the ARPANET had grown and contact information had changed since the May mailing lists.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 363 updates Lists A, B, and C with current names, organizations, phone numbers and addresses for network participants and station agents.
tldr.outcome: The updated distribution lists kept documents reaching the right people across the expanding network.

today: RFC 363 is a historic document superseded by RFC 402. It shows the contact information for ARPANET participants in August 1972.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 363 provides updated mailing lists for distributing network documents across the ARPANET. Like its predecessor RFC 329, it defines three lists: List A for network liaisons at each site, List B for other network participants, and List C for station agents who receive regular mailings.

The document replaces RFC 329 with refreshed contact information reflecting changes in personnel and organizations across the network since May 1972.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an updated version of the address book for sending printed network notes, with changes since the summer began.

sections.title: Distribution Lists
sections.content:
The three lists serve different roles: List A reaches liaisons at each site quickly when sites distribute their own documents. List B reaches non-site participants and researchers at universities and research institutions who need formal network documents. List C reaches Station Agents who receive copies of everything sent to liaisons, plus additional materials from the Network Information Center once per week.

The RFC includes updated entries for sites like BBN-TENEX, MIT-DMCG, Stanford, UCLA, and dozens of other research institutions, government agencies, and universities across North America and Europe.
sections.plainLanguage: List A gets key contacts at each network site, List B reaches researchers elsewhere, and List C reaches helpers who share documents locally.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: This RFC was replaced by RFC 402, which provided the next update as the network continued to grow. Distribution of RFCs by physical mail gradually shifted to electronic delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: This mailing list got updated again a few months later, and eventually the network stopped printing and mailing documents.

references.text: Stanford Research Institute, "ARPA Network Mailing Lists", RFC 329, May 1972.
